6260:
When something is flashy, it is designed or intended to attract attention — usually through bright colors, expensive looks, bold style, or impressive skill. It says: "Look at me. Notice me."

But here's the key: flashy almost always suggests that the attention-seeking is a little too obvious, too loud, or too showy. There's often an unspoken message that the person or thing is trying harder to look impressive than to be genuinely valuable or tasteful.

Think of a car painted in bright gold with neon lights underneath. It screams for attention. That's flashy.

"Flashy" sits somewhere between neutral and mildly negative. It is rarely a pure compliment.

When you call something flashy, you are often hinting that:

  • It prioritizes appearance over substance.
  • It is trying too hard to impress.
  • It may look impressive on the surface but lacks depth or class underneath.

However, context matters. Sometimes people use "flashy" with a hint of admiration — especially when talking about an impressive skill or move. For example, a footballer doing an unexpected trick shot might be called flashy, and the speaker might actually mean it as a compliment. But even then, there's an undercurrent of showing off.

The general rule: if someone calls your outfit flashy, it's not quite a compliment. If someone calls a footballer's skill flashy, it might be.

Flashy can describe a wide range of things:

1. Appearance and style
This is the most common use. Clothes, jewelry, cars, houses — anything that is very loud, bright, bold, or expensive-looking can be called flashy.

  • She walked in wearing a flashy sequined dress.
  • He drove a flashy yellow sports car.
  • The hotel lobby was all marble and gold — very flashy.

2. A person's lifestyle or personality
Someone who spends money openly, wears expensive things to be seen, or constantly shows off their wealth or status is described as flashy.

  • He was a flashy businessman who wore designer suits and carried the latest phone.
  • She lived a flashy life — luxury hotels, private parties, expensive holidays.

3. Skills or moves (especially in sports or performance)
When someone makes a spectacular, eye-catching move — one that's meant to dazzle as much as to be effective — it can be called flashy.

  • The young cricketer played a flashy reverse sweep that surprised everyone.
  • His guitar solo was flashy but a bit too fast to appreciate fully.

Here, flashy is closer to "showy but impressive," with less negative weight.

4. Design and technology
Websites, apps, presentations, or gadgets that prioritize visual appeal over usefulness can also be described as flashy.

  • The presentation was flashy but didn't really explain the product.
  • The app has a flashy interface but it crashes often.

Flashy is gradable — meaning it comes in different strengths:

  • slightly flashy — a bit more bold than usual, but acceptable
  • very flashy — hard to ignore, clearly designed to impress
  • over-the-top flashy — excessive, even embarrassing
How Flashy Differs from Similar Words

Understanding related words helps you use flashy precisely:

Showy — very close to flashy in meaning, but slightly more neutral. It simply means "designed to be noticed." Flashy has a stronger edge of being tasteless or hollow.

Gaudy — this is flashy but worse. Gaudy strongly implies bad taste — too many colors, too much decoration, no sense of elegance. If flashy is a yellow sports car, gaudy is a car covered in plastic diamonds and flashing lights.

Ostentatious — this is the formal, serious word for flashy. It describes something done specifically to show off wealth or status. Ostentatious is what an academic or journalist might write; flashy is what you'd say in everyday conversation.

Flamboyant — this is about personality and behavior. A flamboyant person is bold, dramatic, and expressive in how they dress or act. It can actually be positive or admiring. Flashy is more about the thing itself looking like it's trying to impress; flamboyant is about the person's character being naturally dramatic.

Glitzy — this focuses specifically on superficial sparkle and glamour, especially in entertainment or celebrity culture. It's more playful and less critical than flashy.
Common Collocations (Words Frequently Paired with Flashy)

• flashy car / flashy suit / flashy watch
  • flashy lifestyle
  • flashy move / flashy skills
  • flashy design / flashy website
  • a bit too flashy
  • look flashy / dress flashy

Flashy = eye-catching and showy in a way that feels designed to impress, often at the cost of depth, subtlety, or genuine class.

If you remember that image — something loud and bright waving its arms saying "look at me!" — you will always use this word correctly.
6261:
The flat look is a visual design style where everything appears two-dimensional, clean, and simple — like a sticker on a flat piece of paper. It deliberately avoids any effect that makes things look three-dimensional, textured, or physically real. No fake shine. No shadows. No depth illusions. Just clean shapes, solid colors, and clear typography.

The word "flat" is used quite literally here: the design lies flat, like a drawing, rather than trying to pop out at you or imitate a real physical object.
To Truly Understand "Flat," You First Need to Understand What Came Before It

Before the flat look dominated design, digital interfaces used a style called skeuomorphism (pronounced skyoo-oh-MORE-fizm). This is a big word for a simple idea: making digital things look like their real-world counterparts.

Here are some examples of skeuomorphic design:

  • A notes app that looks like a yellow legal notepad, complete with horizontal ruled lines and a red margin line.
  • A calendar app with fake leather stitching sewn across the top, just like a physical desk calendar.
  • A podcast app that looks like an actual cassette tape or vintage radio.
  • Buttons that look physically raised and three-dimensional, with highlights on top and shadows on the bottom, as if a real light source is shining on them from above.
  • A bookshelf app where digital books sit on a wooden shelf that has a wood-grain texture.

The thinking behind skeuomorphism was logical: people were new to smartphones and computers, so making digital things look familiar — like objects from the real world — helped them understand how to use them intuitively.

But over time, this approach started to feel cluttered, heavy, and gimmicky. Users no longer needed a digital notepad to look like a real notepad to understand what it did. And that's when the flat look took over.
What the Flat Look Actually Looks Like

Here are its defining visual characteristics:

Solid, flat colors — Instead of a color that fades from light to dark (called a gradient), flat design uses one single, clean color. A button is just one shade of blue — not a blue that gets lighter at the top and darker at the bottom to look 3D.

No shadows (or very minimal ones) — There are no drop shadows behind icons or panels, and no inner shadows to make things look sunken or raised.

No textures — There is no imitation of wood, leather, fabric, metal, paper, or any real-world material. Surfaces are plain and clean.

No bevels or embossing — A bevel is when the edge of a button is angled to make it look three-dimensional. Flat design removes this entirely. Buttons look like flat rectangles or pills.

Simple geometric shapes — Circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles. Clean edges. Nothing too ornate or irregular.

Clean typography — The text is easy to read, using modern sans-serif fonts (letters without little feet at the ends). No dramatic decorative fonts.

Generous white space — Empty space is used intentionally and generously to give elements room to breathe and to reduce visual clutter.

Simple, recognizable icons — Icons are stripped down to their most essential recognizable form. A phone icon is just a simple phone shape. A mail icon is just a clean envelope outline.
How and When Flat Design Took Over the World

The flat look didn't appear out of nowhere. Its philosophical roots go back to early 20th-century design movements like Bauhaus (a German school of design from the 1920s that valued simplicity and function over decoration) and the Swiss International Style (also called International Typographic Style), which championed grids, clean typography, and minimalism.

But in the world of digital design, the modern flat look took over through a few key moments:

Microsoft, 2010–2012: Microsoft was the first major tech company to fully commit to flat design in digital products. They introduced their "Metro" design language for Windows Phone 7 in 2010, and then brought it to Windows 8 in 2012. The interface used bold solid colors, simple tiles, and clean typography — a dramatic departure from the glossy, 3D-looking icons that everyone was used to.

Apple, 2013: This was the cultural watershed moment. In 2013, Apple released iOS 7, which completely redesigned the iPhone's interface — throwing out the skeuomorphic style that had defined it since 2007. The new design, led by designer Jony Ive, was flat, light, and simple. The old leather-stitched calendar, the green felt game table, the wooden bookshelf — all gone. Millions of people woke up one day and their iPhone looked entirely different. This shocked many users but signaled to the entire industry that flat was the future.

Google, 2014: Google launched Material Design, their own design system. It's mostly flat but adds a clever twist: it imagines UI elements as sheets of "digital paper" stacked on top of each other. Subtle shadows show which element is layered above another, creating a gentle sense of depth while still looking clean and modern. This became the foundation for Android and all Google apps.

Several forces came together to make flat design the dominant style:

Better screens: As phone and monitor displays became significantly sharper (Retina displays, 4K screens), clean flat designs looked absolutely stunning. There was no need to fake texture because the screens themselves were beautiful.

Users grew up with technology: After years of using smartphones, people no longer needed a digital notepad to look like a real notepad. They already knew what a notes app was.

Performance: Flat designs have smaller file sizes and render faster. No complex textures, no heavy gradient calculations. Pages and apps load more quickly.

Scalability: A flat icon or element looks just as sharp on a tiny phone screen as it does on a giant 4K monitor. Skeuomorphic designs often looked awkward when scaled up or down.

Timelessness: Skeuomorphic designs looked dated very quickly. A digital bookshelf with wood-grain texture felt old almost immediately. Flat designs age much more gracefully.

Content first: With all the decorative clutter removed, the actual content — your photos, your messages, your data — could take center stage instead of competing with visual noise.

You interact with the flat look every single day:

  • Every app icon on your phone is almost certainly flat.
  • Google's apps (Gmail, Maps, Drive, Chrome) all use flat or near-flat design.
  • Apple's iOS — the icons, the control center, the settings menus.
  • Instagram's icon changed from a skeuomorphic camera (with realistic gloss and texture) to a flat, colorful icon in 2016.
  • Microsoft's Windows 11 interface is built on flat design principles.
  • Nearly every modern website you visit uses flat buttons, flat navigation bars, and solid color sections.
  • Many major brand logos simplified to flat versions — Google, Airbnb, Uber, and many more have done this over the past decade.
The Downsides of the Flat Look

Flat design is not without its critics or real problems:

Reduced affordance: In design, "affordance" means the visual cues that tell you what something does. A 3D-looking button looks like something you can press. A flat rectangle is less obvious. This is why some early flat apps confused users — they couldn't always tell what was clickable and what wasn't.

Visual similarity: When everyone uses the same minimalist style, many apps and websites start to look alike. The flat look can sometimes feel generic or soulless.

Weak hierarchy: Without shadows and depth to guide the eye, designers have to work harder to establish visual hierarchy — to show which element is most important on a page.

Cold aesthetic: Some users and industries (luxury goods, for example) find the flat look too sterile. They prefer warmth, texture, and richness.
Flat Design Evolves: "Semi-Flat" and Material Design

Designers noticed the usability issues and started evolving flat design rather than abandoning it. Two important evolutions emerged:

Flat 2.0 / Semi-flat design: This reintroduces very subtle shadows and depth cues — just enough to distinguish interactive buttons from static text, and to show hierarchy between elements. It's still clean and modern, but it borrows just a tiny bit from the 3D world to solve practical usability problems.

Material Design (Google): As mentioned earlier, Material Design is built on the metaphor of stacked paper. Each UI element exists at a specific "elevation" — and soft, realistic shadows indicate which elements are higher or lower. It's mostly flat but uses depth strategically and logically. A floating action button (the round + button you see in many Android apps) casts a shadow because it sits "above" the content beneath it. This gives users subtle but meaningful spatial cues.
The Flat Look in Other Fields

While flat look is most discussed in graphic and UI/UX design, the term appears in other areas too:

Photography and Videography: Here, a "flat look" or "flat profile" means something quite different but related. Filmmakers and photographers often shoot footage using a special camera setting called a log profile (like Sony's S-Log or Canon's C-Log). This makes the footage look intentionally dull, gray, low-contrast, and desaturated — literally flat-looking. This is done on purpose, not because they want a boring final result. A flat image captures a much wider range of light and dark detail (called dynamic range) that would otherwise be lost. Later, in the editing stage (called color grading), the colorist takes that flat, raw footage and transforms it into rich, cinematic colors. Almost every professional film, TV show, and high-end YouTube video is shot this way.

Fashion and Makeup: A "flat look" in fashion or makeup can mean an outfit or makeup style that lacks visual dimension — for example, a matte (non-shiny) makeup look with no shimmer is sometimes called flat. The related term "flat lay" refers to a popular photography style where clothing, accessories, or food items are arranged and photographed from directly above, lying flat on a surface.
The Quickest Way to Remember All of This

Think of it this way: skeuomorphic design says, "let me make this digital thing look like a real-world object." Flat design says, "let me make this digital thing look like the best possible version of itself — simple, clear, and purposeful."

The flat look is the visual language of modern digital design. It prioritizes clarity, speed, and content over decoration and imitation. It's why your phone's interface looks the way it does today, why most logos got simpler over the last decade, and why when you open almost any app, you're greeted with clean shapes, solid colors, and breathing room — instead of virtual wood grain and plastic buttons.
6262:
Before diving into the details, here is the core idea to hold in your mind:

"Flat out" is an informal English expression that generally signals something done to its fullest, most extreme degree — whether that's maximum speed, maximum effort, absolute directness, or complete exhaustion.

Think of the word "flat." A flat surface has no bumps, no curves, no middle ground. When something is flat, it is all the way at one extreme. That feeling — of being pushed to the absolute limit, of leaving no room for doubt — runs through every meaning of "flat out."
Meaning 1: At Maximum Speed or Effort

This is the most common and widely understood meaning. When you do something flat out, you are doing it as fast as you possibly can, or with every bit of effort you have — holding nothing back.

Think of a car's accelerator pedal pressed all the way down, lying completely flat against the floor. The engine is running at full power. That image is exactly what "flat out" captures here.

Examples:

  • "The runners sprinted flat out in the final 100 metres." — They ran as fast as their bodies would allow.
  • "She worked flat out for two weeks to finish the project before the deadline." — She gave it everything she had, with no breaks or holding back.
  • "The car was going flat out on the motorway." — It was travelling at top speed.
  • "We were going flat out just to keep up with the demand." — We were working at our absolute maximum capacity.

Notice that "flat out" here works as an adverb — it describes how something is done. It answers the question: To what degree? Answer: to the maximum degree.

A good way to remember this: imagine running a race and someone shouts "Go flat out!" They mean: run like your life depends on it. Leave nothing in the tank.
Meaning 2: Completely, Absolutely, Without Any Doubt

This is extremely common in American English and is becoming more widely used everywhere. In this sense, "flat out" means completely or absolutely — but with an extra flavour of directness or bluntness. There is no softening, no maybe, no "sort of." The statement is laid completely flat — no curves, no exceptions.

This meaning is very often used when someone refuses, denies, or says something very directly.

Examples:

  • "He flat out refused to apologise." — He refused without any hesitation or polite softening. A flat, total refusal.
  • "She flat out lied to my face." — She didn't bend the truth a little. She completely and directly lied.
  • "I flat out don't believe you." — I believe you zero percent. Not a little sceptical — completely unconvinced.
  • "They flat out denied any involvement." — Their denial was total. No "we're not sure" or "perhaps." Just a direct, complete denial.
  • "I told him flat out that it wasn't going to work." — I told him plainly and directly, without softening the message.

In this sense, "flat out" works almost like the words completely, absolutely, or point-blank. But it carries a stronger feeling of directness — almost like a punch. When someone says something "flat out," they are not dancing around it. They say it plainly and with finality.
Meaning 3: Totally Exhausted (Mainly British English)

In British English especially, if someone is flat out, they may be completely exhausted — so tired that they are lying flat and cannot do anything more. The image here is of a person flopped flat on a bed or sofa, unable to move.

Examples:

  • "After the marathon, she was flat out on the sofa for the rest of the evening." — She was completely wiped out.
  • "The children were flat out by seven o'clock." — The kids had used up all their energy and were asleep or resting.
  • "I got home and was just flat out — I couldn't even eat dinner." — Completely drained of energy.

This meaning connects to the visual of lying flat — your body is fully horizontal, completely surrendered to tiredness.
Meaning 4: Extremely Busy (Mainly British English)

This is another British usage, closely related to Meaning 1 (maximum effort). If someone is flat out, they are so busy that they are working at their maximum capacity — there is no free moment at all.

Examples:

  • "Sorry I haven't called — I've been flat out at work all week." — I have been working non-stop and had no time.
  • "We're flat out trying to fill all the orders before Christmas." — We are working at full capacity with no breathing room.
  • "The hospital staff were flat out during the crisis." — They were under extreme pressure with no spare time or energy.

You can think of this as a combination of Meanings 1 and 3 — you are working at full speed (Meaning 1), and as a result, you feel completely drained (Meaning 3).
Where Did "Flat Out" Come From?

Understanding the origin makes the idiom much easier to remember.

The most likely origin comes from engines and machinery, particularly in the early days of motor racing and aviation. A throttle — the device that controls how much fuel an engine receives — is a lever or pedal. When you push that lever or pedal all the way down, it lies completely flat. At that point, the engine is running at full power. Mechanics and racing drivers began using "flat out" to describe this state of maximum engine performance, and the phrase soon moved into everyday language to mean going at full speed or effort.

There is also a vivid horse racing image behind it. When a horse gallops at its absolute fastest, it stretches its entire body forward — neck extended, legs reaching — so that it appears almost completely horizontal, almost flat. A horse running "flat out" is giving everything it has.

The "absolutely/completely" meaning likely grew from the same root idea: something completely flat has no humps or bumps — no exceptions, no doubts, no softening. A flat denial is an absolute denial.
How "Flat Out" Fits Into a Sentence (Grammar)

"Flat out" is used as an adverb. This means it modifies a verb, an adjective, or the whole statement. You do not use it as a noun or as the main verb.

Here are the most common sentence patterns:

Pattern 1: Subject + flat out + verb

  • "He flat out refused."
  • "She flat out lied."

Pattern 2: Subject + verb + flat out

  • "The car was going flat out."
  • "She worked flat out."
  • "They were running flat out."

Pattern 3: Subject + was/is/be + flat out

  • "I was flat out exhausted." (American: completely exhausted)
  • "She was flat out on the sofa." (British: lying flat/exhausted)
  • "We've been flat out all week." (British: extremely busy)

Pattern 4: Go flat out
This is a very common phrase on its own:

  • "Just go flat out and see what you can do." — Give it absolutely everything.
  • "We went flat out from the very beginning."
British English vs. American English — Key Differences

While "flat out" is used in both British and American English, there are some differences worth knowing.

In American English, the dominant meaning is "completely/absolutely" (Meaning 2). Americans very frequently use "flat out" before a verb like refuse, deny, lie, say, tell — to signal bluntness and totality.

In British English, all four meanings are used, but Meanings 3 and 4 (exhausted and very busy) are especially common. A British person saying "I've been flat out" most often means they have been extremely busy or tired, not that they have been going at top speed.

Meaning 1 (maximum speed/effort) is understood and used on both sides.
The Register — When Is It Appropriate to Use?

"Flat out" is informal and colloquial. This means you would use it in:

  • Casual conversations with friends and family
  • Informal writing, like text messages or personal emails
  • Sports commentary
  • Storytelling and narrative writing

You would generally avoid it in:

  • Formal academic essays
  • Official business reports
  • Legal or professional documents

It is perfectly natural and common in everyday spoken English, and nobody would think twice about hearing it in casual speech.
Common Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Confusing "flat out" with "flat out wrong."
You might sometimes hear "that's flat out wrong" — this is just Meaning 2 applied to "wrong." It means "that is completely wrong." It is not a separate special phrase, just the same meaning used with an adjective.

Mistake 2: Using it in formal writing.
Because it is idiomatic and informal, dropping it into a formal essay would sound odd. Stick to "completely," "absolutely," or "at maximum capacity" in formal contexts.

Mistake 3: Forgetting it can describe a state, not just an action.
People sometimes think "flat out" only describes doing something fast. But remember it can describe a state — being tired, being busy — not just a speed or action.
A Quick Summary of All Meanings

To bring it all together in plain terms:

"Flat out" means at full speed or effort — like a racing car with the accelerator pressed all the way down. It also means completely and directly, without holding back — like a flat, straight denial that leaves no room for doubt. In British English especially, it also means completely exhausted — like lying flat on the floor — or extremely busy, working at full capacity with no breathing space.

The thread connecting all these meanings is the same: flat = at the extreme, with nothing held back, no middle ground, no softening. Whether you are running flat out, flat out refusing something, or flat out exhausted, the emotion is always the same: you have reached the absolute limit.
Final Examples to Cement It All

Read these final examples slowly and think about which meaning fits each one:

  • "The athlete was going flat out for the finish line." → Maximum speed.
  • "I flat out forgot your birthday and I'm so sorry." → Completely, absolutely — a direct admission.
  • "She flat out told him she wasn't interested." → Directly and plainly, without softening.
  • "I've been flat out all day — I haven't even had lunch." → Extremely busy (British).
  • "After moving all those boxes, I was flat out on the couch." → Completely exhausted.
  • "They went flat out to save the business." → With everything they had — maximum effort.

Once you can read those sentences and feel the meaning without even thinking about it, you have truly understood "flat out."
6263: "Flat-footed" has one literal meaning and several figurative meanings. Understanding all of them will make you fully confident with this word.

This is the most basic meaning. A person is described as flat-footed when the arch of their foot is very low or completely absent, causing the entire bottom of the foot to press flat against the ground when they stand or walk.

Most people have a visible curve on the inner side of their foot when they stand — that curve is the arch. A flat-footed person has little or no such curve. The foot sits fully flat on the floor.

"The doctor confirmed that the child was flat-footed and recommended special shoe insoles."

This is a real, common physical condition. It can sometimes cause pain or awkward walking, which is precisely why the word traveled into figurative use — because flat-footed walking looks unsteady and ungraceful.
Meaning 2 — Caught Unprepared or Off Guard (the most common figurative use)

This is the meaning you will encounter most often in everyday English, especially in the phrase "caught flat-footed."

It means to be taken completely by surprise, in a situation you were not prepared for — so surprised, in fact, that you cannot react quickly or properly. Like someone caught standing flat on their feet when they should have been ready to move.

Think of it this way: a person who is alert and ready to act is "on their toes." A person who is flat-footed is the opposite — their feet are flat on the ground, they are not ready, and they cannot spring into action.

"The journalist's tough question caught the politician completely flat-footed — he just stumbled over his words."

"The sudden price increase caught the company flat-footed, and they had no plan in place."

"She was caught flat-footed when her boss asked her to present right away — she hadn't prepared anything."

The key feeling here is: surprise + unpreparedness + inability to respond well. All three are usually present.
Meaning 3 — Clumsy, Heavy, and Graceless in Movement

This meaning stays close to the literal idea. If you describe someone's movement or style as flat-footed, you mean they move in a heavy, slow, clumsy, ungraceful way — without lightness, quickness, or agility.

This is used both about physical movement and about the way someone does their work or plays a sport.

"The defender looked flat-footed as the striker raced past him."

"His dancing was flat-footed and awkward — he had no sense of rhythm."

The image is of someone plodding along with both feet heavy on the ground, rather than moving lightly and swiftly.
Meaning 4 — Direct, Blunt, and Straightforward (sometimes too blunt)

When "flat-footed" describes someone's speech, manner, or approach, it can mean they are very direct and plain — with no softening, no tact, no elegance. They just say the thing as it is, flatly, without any finesse.

This can be neutral (simply direct) or slightly negative (blunt to the point of being rude or crude).

"He gave a flat-footed refusal — no explanation, no apology, just 'No.'"

"Her flat-footed comment about his work embarrassed him in front of the group."

Think of it as the verbal version of heavy, graceless movement — the person is not dancing around the subject with care; they are stomping straight through it.

In a more critical sense, "flat-footed" can describe something — a piece of writing, a performance, a plan, an argument — that is lacking imagination, creativity, or spark. It is pedestrian, obvious, and flat. It does not surprise you or impress you. It just sits there, going nowhere.

"The film had a flat-footed script — every line felt predictable and tired."

"The manager's flat-footed response to the crisis showed a complete lack of creative thinking."

"It was a flat-footed speech — safe, dull, and instantly forgettable."

This meaning connects to the others: just as a flat-footed person moves without grace or energy, a flat-footed idea or piece of work has no energy, no lift, no spark.

It helps to see these meanings as a family:

The literal meaning (feet flat on the ground, no arch) gives birth to all the others. Flat feet suggest heaviness, lack of readiness, no spring, no grace. From there:

  • No readiness → caught off guard
  • No grace in movement → clumsy
  • No finesse in speaking → blunt and tactless
  • No spark or lift in work → dull and uninspired

Once you see that core image — a person standing heavy and immovable, with no lightness or agility — all five meanings feel natural and logical.

ContextWhat it means
PhysicalHaving flat feet (no arch)
ReactionCaught unprepared and unable to respond
MovementClumsy, heavy, graceless
Speech/mannerBlunt and direct, lacking tact
Ideas/workDull, unimaginative, uninspired

The meaning you will use and hear by far the most is "caught flat-footed" — surprised and unprepared. Master that one first, and the others will follow naturally.
6264:
Imagine a hospital room. A patient is connected to a heart monitor — a machine that tracks the electrical activity of the heart and draws it on a screen as a moving line. When the heart beats normally, this line moves up and down rhythmically, creating a series of sharp peaks and valleys. It looks alive because it is alive.

Now imagine the heart stops. Completely. No beats, no electrical activity, nothing. That moving, jumping line instantly collapses into a perfectly still, perfectly horizontal line — a flat line. The machine also lets out a single, unbroken tone. This is the image that gave birth to the verb.

To flatline = to produce or become that flat line.

1. The medical meaning (literal)

In medicine, to flatline means for a person's heart to stop beating entirely, resulting in that flat horizontal line on the monitor. It is another way of saying someone has gone into cardiac arrest or has clinically died.

"The patient flatlined on the operating table."
(The patient's heart stopped beating.)

It can also refer to the moment of death more broadly — not just the heart, but all brain and bodily activity ceasing. Doctors and nurses use it directly in clinical settings, but it has also become part of everyday language because of its appearance in films, TV dramas, and news.

Importantly, flatlining does not always mean permanent death. In many medical contexts, someone who flatlines can sometimes be revived with CPR, defibrillators, or emergency drugs. So you will often hear:

"He flatlined for two minutes before the team brought him back."

This is why the word carries an edge of extreme danger and crisis — it describes the boundary between life and death.

2. The figurative meaning (extended use)

This is where the word becomes truly versatile. Because the flat line on a monitor represents zero activity, zero growth, zero change, people began using "flatline" to describe anything that stops moving, growing, or progressing — especially after a period when it was active or rising.

Think of it this way: just as the heart monitor line goes flat when life stops, any graph, chart, or measurement "flatlines" when its numbers stop changing and stretch out in a flat, motionless direction.

This figurative use appears most commonly in:

Economics and business:

"Sales flatlined in the third quarter."

(Sales neither grew nor fell — they were completely stagnant.)

"The economy flatlined after years of steady growth."

(Growth came to a halt.)

Politics:

"The candidate's poll numbers have flatlined."

(Support has stopped growing and is stuck.)

Personal progress or careers:

"His development as a musician seemed to flatline after his second album."

(He stopped improving or evolving.)

Technology or products:

"User engagement flatlined six months after launch."

(People stopped interacting with it.)

The key idea across all these uses is stagnation — a complete lack of upward or downward movement. The thing in question has, in a sense, "died" in terms of momentum, energy, or progress.

3. A stronger figurative meaning: to fail or collapse

Sometimes — though less commonly — "flatline" is used to mean something has completely failed, collapsed, or died in a figurative sense, not just stagnated. Here, the emphasis shifts from "no movement" to "it's finished."

"The project flatlined due to lack of funding."

(The project died — it did not merely stall.)

"Without reform, the industry will flatline."

(The industry will collapse or cease to function meaningfully.)

In this usage, the speaker is borrowing the death imagery more directly — comparing the failure of something to the death of a person.
The emotional weight of the word

"Flatline" is not a neutral word. It carries a sense of alarm, crisis, and finality. When someone uses it — whether in a hospital or in a business meeting — it signals that something serious has happened or is at risk of happening. It is more dramatic than simply saying "stop" or "stagnate."

Compare:

  • "Growth has stopped." → Neutral, plain.
  • "Growth has flatlined." → Vivid, alarming, suggests urgency.

This is why writers, journalists, and speakers reach for "flatline" when they want to make an impact. It transforms a dry fact into something you can almost see and hear — that still, flat line, that single unbroken tone.
Summary of meanings at a glance

ContextWhat it means
  • Medical, literal: The heart stops beating entirely; the person is clinically dying or dead.
  • Figurative – stagnation: Something stops growing or changing; it becomes completely flat and motionless, like a graph with a horizontal line.
  • Figurative – failure: Something collapses or dies entirely, losing all function or viability.

At its heart (no pun intended), to flatline means to go flat — to lose all the movement, rhythm, and vitality that once defined something. Whether it is a heartbeat, an economy, a career, or a project, when something flatlines, the life has gone out of it. The word is powerful precisely because it borrows its imagery directly from death, forcing you to feel the gravity of what it describes, even when the subject is as abstract as quarterly revenue or political popularity.
6265:
To flatter someone means to praise them in a way that is more generous, more enthusiastic, or more exaggerated than the truth really warrants — often to make them feel good, or to get something in return.

At the heart of the word is a kind of pleasant dishonesty. The praise isn't necessarily a lie, but it's stretched beyond what is accurate or deserved.
Meaning 1 — To Praise Someone Excessively (Often with a Hidden Goal)

This is the most common meaning. When you flatter someone, you say very nice things about them — their looks, their work, their intelligence — in a way that is either exaggerated or not entirely sincere. The key is that the praise is inflated.

Why do people flatter? Usually because they want something. They want the other person to like them, to help them, to give them something, or simply to feel pleased. Flattery is often a social tool.

Examples:

  • "He flattered his boss by constantly telling her she was the most brilliant manager in the company — hoping to get a promotion."
  • "She flattered the interviewer by saying his questions were the most insightful she had ever heard."
  • "Stop flattering me and just tell me honestly what you think of my work."

Notice the pattern: the praise goes a little (or a lot) beyond what is genuinely meant.
Meaning 2 — When Something Makes You Look Better Than You Actually Are

This is a very important second meaning, and it doesn't involve people praising each other at all. Here, an object, a situation, or a condition does the "flattering." It means something — clothing, lighting, a photo, an angle — makes a person appear more attractive, slimmer, taller, or more impressive than they truly are.

Examples:

  • "That dress really flatters her — it makes her look elegant."
  • "The soft lighting in the restaurant flattered everyone; people looked younger and more glowing than usual."
  • "That photo doesn't flatter him at all — he looks much better in person."
  • "The wide-angle lens flatters the apartment by making it look much more spacious than it is."

In this sense, "flatter" is not about words or intentions. It's about how something creates a more favourable impression than reality. A dress flatters your figure. A good camera angle flatters your face. Evening light flatters a landscape.

This is why you'll often hear: "That colour is very flattering on you" — meaning it makes you look particularly good.

The phrase "flatter yourself" is used when someone has an overly positive belief about themselves — usually an unrealistic one.

It means: you are giving yourself more credit than you deserve; you are imagining something favourable about yourself that isn't quite true.

Examples:

  • "Don't flatter yourself — she didn't cancel the meeting because of you. She was just busy."
  • "He flatters himself that he is a great singer, but the audience clearly disagrees."
  • "I wouldn't flatter yourself into thinking they need you — they have plenty of other options."

This usage almost always carries a tone of gentle mockery or correction. You're telling someone: stop believing this flattering story you've told yourself.

"Flatter" carries a mildly negative connotation in most uses. It implies insincerity, exaggeration, or self-interest. When you call someone a flatterer, you're saying they give hollow praise. When you say someone is just flattering you, you're suggesting their praise shouldn't be taken seriously.

However, this negative shade isn't always strong. Sometimes people say "I'm flattered" (see below) with genuine warmth.

When someone says "I am flattered," they mean they feel pleased, touched, or honoured by what was said to them — even if they suspect it might be slightly exaggerated.

Examples:

  • "I'm flattered that you think so highly of my writing."
  • "She was flattered when he asked her to lead the project."
  • "He seemed flattered by all the attention."

This is the receiving end of flattery. You feel a warm glow, a sense of being valued. It doesn't necessarily mean you fully believe the praise — just that it made you feel good.
The Crucial Difference: Flatter vs. Compliment

This distinction matters a lot.

A compliment is honest, accurate praise. You say something good because you genuinely mean it.

  • "Your presentation was well-structured and clear." → a compliment.

Flattery is praise that is exaggerated, excessive, or strategically given to please someone or gain their favour.

  • "Your presentation was absolutely the most incredible thing I've ever seen in my life — you are a genius!" → flattery.

The difference is one of sincerity and proportion. Compliments are measured and true. Flattery overshoots the truth, often intentionally.

You'll frequently see flattering used to describe things:

  • A flattering portrait — one that makes the subject look better than they do in real life.
  • A flattering review — one that praises a book or film generously (sometimes more than it deserves).
  • A flattering light — soft, warm light that makes people look more beautiful.
  • A not-very-flattering comment — a remark that, accidentally or deliberately, makes someone look bad.

SituationWhat "flatter" means
A person flatters another personThey give exaggerated, often insincere praise — usually to gain something
Clothing/lighting/a photo flatters someoneIt makes them look more attractive than they usually do
Someone flatters themselvesThey believe something too good about themselves
Someone feels flatteredThey feel pleased and honoured by praise they received
A Few Final Examples Across All Meanings

1. "He flattered the professor all semester, hoping she'd give him a higher grade." — insincere praise with a motive.
  2. "Don't flatter me — I know this essay has problems." — stop giving me praise I don't deserve.
  3. "The black jacket really flatters your shoulders." — clothing makes you look better.
  4. "Don't flatter yourself into thinking you were the reason she stayed." — you're believing something too good about yourself.
  5. "I'm deeply flattered by your kind words." — I feel honoured and touched.
  6. "That photo is extremely flattering — she looks like a model." — the photo presents her in an unusually favourable way.

The word "flatter" always orbits the same idea: creating a more favourable impression than reality strictly supports — whether through words, through appearance, or through self-belief. Sometimes it's warm and harmless. Often it's strategic or insincere. Occasionally it's a gentle correction when someone thinks too well of themselves.
6266:
Flattery is excessive, insincere praise given to someone — not because you truly mean it, but because you want to get something from them, make them like you, or make them feel good for your own benefit.

The single most important thing to understand about flattery is this: it looks like a compliment on the outside, but it is not the same thing. A genuine compliment is honest. Flattery is not.
The Heart of the Word: Sincerity vs. Strategy

Imagine two scenarios:

Your friend works hard on a painting for months. You look at it and say, "This is truly beautiful — you have a real gift." You mean every word. That is a compliment.

Now imagine your boss has just written a dull, mediocre report. You want a promotion, so you walk up and say, "This is the most brilliant piece of writing I've ever read!" You don't believe that — not even close. You're saying it to win favour. That is flattery.

The difference is not the words. The difference is the truth and the motive behind them. Flattery is praise that is:

  • Exaggerated — blown way out of proportion
  • Insincere — the speaker doesn't truly believe it
  • Self-serving — the speaker has a hidden goal: to please, manipulate, or gain something

People use flattery for many reasons, and it's worth knowing all of them:

To gain favour. Someone might shower their boss with flattery to get a raise, a promotion, or to avoid getting in trouble.

To manipulate. A skilled flatterer knows that when people feel praised, they lower their guard and become easier to influence. Salespeople, politicians, and con artists often use flattery as a tool.

To smooth things over. Someone might use flattery to calm an angry person, or to make an awkward situation more comfortable.

Out of social habit. Some people flatter others simply because they're people-pleasers — they've learned that saying nice things (even untrue ones) keeps everyone around them happy with them.

To seduce or charm. Flattery is a classic tool of romance and seduction, where one person overwhelms another with compliments to win their affection.
How Flattery Feels — and Why It Works

Here is something fascinating: flattery works even when people know it's flattery. Research and everyday experience both show this. When someone tells you that you're intelligent, talented, or attractive — even if a small part of you suspects they don't mean it — it still feels good. And that good feeling can cloud your judgment.

This is why flattery is considered a form of manipulation. It exploits a basic human weakness: we all want to be admired. A skilled flatterer targets this desire and uses it to their advantage.

Since flattery wears the costume of a compliment, it can be hard to spot. Here are the telltale signs:

It is over the top. Genuine compliments are usually specific and measured. Flattery tends to be extreme — words like "the most amazing," "absolutely perfect," "no one could ever do this better."

It comes at a convenient time. Notice when the praise arrives. If someone is suddenly very complimentary right before asking you for a favour, that is a red flag.

It is vague. Flattery often praises in broad strokes without specific reasons. "You're just incredible!" tells you nothing real. A genuine compliment usually has a reason: "The way you explained that problem was so clear — I finally understood it."

It doesn't match reality. If someone praises your average cooking as "the best meal I've ever eaten in my life," something is off.

The flatterer benefits. Ask yourself: does this person gain something by making me feel good right now?
The Fine Line: When Does a Compliment Become Flattery?

This is one of the trickiest aspects of the word, so pay close attention.

Not every exaggerated or enthusiastic compliment is flattery. If a parent says to their child, "You are the most wonderful kid in the world!" — is that flattery? Not really. It is an expression of love, not a strategy to get something. Intent matters enormously.

The word "flattery" almost always carries a negative or suspicious tone. When someone says, "That's just flattery," they mean: "Don't believe that — there's an ulterior motive."

However, there is one situation where flattery is used more lightly and without any dark intent — simply as a charming, playful over-compliment with no manipulation involved. In this case, it can even be affectionate. But in most serious usage, flattery implies dishonesty and self-interest.
Common Phrases and Expressions With This Word

"Flattery will get you nowhere" — said to someone whose praise you can see through, telling them it won't work on you.

"Flattery will get you everywhere" — the ironic, humorous flip side; said jokingly to acknowledge that you enjoyed the compliment.

"I'm immune to flattery" — meaning: excessive or insincere praise has no effect on me.

"Don't fall for flattery" — a warning to someone not to be manipulated by nice-sounding but insincere words.

Since you're learning, it helps to know how this word connects to its family:

  • Flattery (noun) — the act or instance of giving excessive, insincere praise. "His flattery was so obvious that everyone in the room saw through it."
  • To flatter (verb) — the action of doing it. "She flattered him to get what she wanted."
  • A flatterer (noun) — a person who regularly uses flattery. "He was a known flatterer in the office — always praising the boss."
  • Flattering (adjective) — can mean either "containing flattery" OR simply "making someone look or seem better." For example, a flattering photograph is one that makes you look good, without any dishonest intent behind the word in that context.
The Moral Weight of the Word

Flattery is generally considered a character flaw or at least a morally questionable behaviour. A person who relies on flattery is seen as dishonest, fake, or untrustworthy. Throughout history, philosophers and writers have warned against both giving and receiving flattery.

The danger of flattery is not just that it's dishonest — it's that it can distort your thinking. If a leader surrounds themselves with flatterers who only say what the leader wants to hear, that leader begins to lose touch with reality. This is sometimes called being surrounded by yes-men — people who flatter rather than give honest feedback.

Honest criticism, however uncomfortable, is far more valuable than comfortable flattery — because it is real.

If you had to sum up "flattery" in a single sentence, it would be this:

Flattery is praise that sounds like a compliment but is driven by dishonesty or self-interest, not by genuine admiration.

Keep that in your mind, and you will always understand the word — no matter what context you encounter it in.
6267: Flatulent is an adjective that describes anything to do with gas that builds up inside the digestive system — the stomach and intestines — and eventually needs to escape from the body, either as a burp from the mouth or as gas passed from the rear end. You may know this more informally as "having gas" or "being gassy."
How It Is Used — The Literal Meaning

The word works in two closely related ways when used literally:

1. To describe a person

When someone is called flatulent, it means they are experiencing an uncomfortable buildup of gas in their digestive system, causing them to pass that gas frequently or excessively.

"He felt flatulent after eating too quickly and gulping down air with his meal."

"The patient visited the doctor complaining of feeling bloated and flatulent for several days."

It's worth noting that the word carries a slightly clinical or formal tone. A doctor would comfortably use "flatulent" when talking to a patient, but in casual everyday conversation, people are far more likely to say "gassy" instead. Both mean the same thing — "flatulent" just sounds more medical and formal.

2. To describe food or drink

When a food or drink is described as flatulent, it means that particular item is known to cause gas in the digestive system of the person who eats or drinks it.

"Beans, onions, and cabbage are notoriously flatulent foods."

"Carbonated drinks can be flatulent for many people."

So the word doesn't only describe the person experiencing gas — it can also describe the cause of the gas. This is a useful and common application of the word.
The Figurative Meaning — A Very Important Secondary Sense

"Flatulent" has a second meaning that has nothing to do with the body. When applied to speech, writing, or ideas, flatulent means pompous, inflated, and full of empty, impressive-sounding words that carry very little real meaning or substance.

Think about it this way: gas takes up a lot of space but has no weight or value. In the same way, flatulent language sounds big and important, but when you look closely, there is almost nothing of real value inside it. It is all air.

"The politician gave a flatulent speech full of grand promises but offered no concrete plan."

"His writing style was flatulent — long, elaborate sentences that ultimately said very little."

"The professor's flatulent lecture left students more confused than when they arrived."

This figurative use is common in literary criticism and journalism. When a critic calls a book or a speech "flatulent," it is not a compliment — they are saying it is bloated, pretentious, and hollow.
The Relationship Between the Two Meanings

The connection between the literal and figurative meanings is intentional and quite elegant. In both cases, the central idea is something that takes up space without having real substance. Digestive gas fills up the body without nourishing it. Flatulent language fills up a speech or a page without informing or enlightening anyone. The figurative meaning is essentially a metaphor built directly on the literal one.

• In medical or clinical contexts, "flatulent" is a perfectly neutral, professional term.
  • In everyday conversation, it is a somewhat formal or even polite way of referring to something people often joke about or find embarrassing. Using "flatulent" instead of blunter alternatives makes the reference sound more dignified.
  • In literary or critical writing, the figurative sense (pompous, inflated) is widely used and respected.

The word is never considered offensive or vulgar. It sits comfortably in formal writing, medical discussions, and serious literary criticism alike.
Related Word Forms You Should Know

• Flatulence (noun) — the condition of having excessive gas in the digestive system, or the gas itself. "The doctor asked about his flatulence."
  • Flatulently (adverb) — in a flatulent manner. "He spoke flatulently, padding every idea with unnecessary words."
  • Flatus (noun, formal/medical) — the actual gas produced and expelled from the digestive tract. This one is strictly medical and rarely used outside clinical settings.

SenseWhat It MeansExample

Literal (person): Having or producing too much digestive gas.
Literal (food): Causing digestive gas.
Figurative (speech/writing): Puffed up with empty words; pompous and hollow.

In all cases, the unifying idea is the same — something inflated and without real substance.
6268:
To flaunt something means to display it very openly and deliberately so that other people notice it — usually out of pride, and often in a way that feels excessive or showy.

It's not just having something. It's making sure everyone around you sees that you have it.

Three things are almost always present when someone flaunts:

1. It is deliberate.
You are not accidentally showing something. You are consciously putting it on display. You want people to look.

2. There is a sense of pride — sometimes even arrogance.
The person flaunting feels good about what they're showing. They are not shy about it at all.

3. It is excessive or showy.
This is what separates flaunting from simply "showing." Simply wearing a gold necklace is not flaunting. But constantly touching it, angling it toward people, and talking about how expensive it was — that's flaunting.

Flaunt is mostly a negative word. When you describe someone as flaunting something, you are usually suggesting they are being a little too showy — almost rubbing it in others' faces. There is a subtle judgment in the word: this person is showing off more than is tasteful.

However, occasionally it is used in an empowering or even admiring way — for example, when someone is celebrating a person's confidence: "She's not ashamed of her body — she flaunts it!" Even here, though, the "showy" quality of the word remains. The difference is just that the showing off is being cheered rather than criticized.

As a rule of thumb: if you replace "flaunt" with "show off" in a sentence and it still sounds right, you've understood the word correctly.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Flaunted?

Almost anything a person feels proud of — or wants others to think they should be proud of:

  • Wealth — expensive cars, designer clothes, luxury items
  • Beauty or physical appearance — someone who dresses to attract maximum attention to their looks
  • Success or achievements — constantly mentioning awards, grades, or accomplishments
  • Relationships or social status — name-dropping famous friends, showing off a partner
  • Talent or intelligence — going out of the way to demonstrate a skill when it wasn't needed

• He bought a sports car just to flaunt his wealth in front of his neighbors.
    He didn't need the car. He bought it to make sure people noticed how rich he is.
  • She flaunted her promotion by casually mentioning her new title in every conversation.
    She kept bringing it up on purpose so people would be impressed.
  • The actor flaunted his muscular physique on the red carpet.
    He dressed and posed in a way that was clearly designed to draw attention to his body.
  • Don't flaunt your success in front of those who are still struggling.
    Don't shove your achievements in people's faces when they are going through hard times — it's unkind.
A Very Important Warning: Flaunt vs. Flout

This is one of the most common mistakes even native English speakers make, so pay close attention.

Flaunt and flout sound similar but mean completely different things.

  • Flaunt = to show something off proudly (display)
  • Flout = to openly disobey or disregard a rule or convention (defy)

Wrong: "The students were flaunting the school rules."
Right: "The students were flouting the school rules." (They were breaking/ignoring the rules — not showing them off.)

Right: "The students were flaunting their new uniforms." (They were proudly showing off their uniforms.)

A helpful trick: think of flaunt → flauntingly beautiful (showing off beauty). Think of flout → flouting the law (defying the law). They are completely separate ideas.
One Sentence to Remember It Forever
To flaunt is to show something off in a way that is too loud, too obvious, and a little too proud — because you want people to notice.
6269:
A flavoring is any substance that is added to food or drink specifically to give it a taste, to change its existing taste, or to make its taste stronger.

The key word here is added. A flavoring is not the food itself — it is something brought in from outside, mixed in or applied, with one purpose: to affect how the food tastes or smells.

Taste and smell are deeply connected. A large part of what we experience as "flavor" actually comes through our nose, not just our tongue. This is why flavorings often have a strong aroma as well as a taste. Vanilla extract, for example, smells intensely of vanilla — and that smell is a big part of why it makes baked goods taste the way they do. So when you read that a flavoring affects taste, understand that it almost always affects smell too.

A natural flavoring is one that comes directly from a plant, animal, or other natural source — without being created artificially in a lab.

Examples:

  • Vanilla extract — made from real vanilla beans soaked in alcohol. Added to cakes, cookies, and ice cream.
  • Lemon zest — the grated outer skin of a lemon, used to add a bright citrus flavor to food.
  • Cinnamon — a spice from tree bark, used as a flavoring in desserts and warm drinks.
  • Peppermint oil — pressed from mint leaves, used to flavor toothpaste, candies, and teas.
  • Almond extract — comes from almonds, used in pastries.

These are considered natural because they originate from something found in nature and are not synthetically manufactured.

An artificial flavoring (also called a synthetic flavoring) is one that is created chemically in a laboratory. It is designed to imitate the taste of a natural thing — often very accurately — but it does not actually come from that natural source.

For example:

  • Artificial vanilla flavoring (called vanillin) is made from wood pulp or petrochemicals. It smells and tastes like vanilla, but no vanilla bean was used.
  • Artificial strawberry flavoring used in candies is a mix of chemicals engineered to taste like strawberry, but contains no real strawberries.

Artificial flavorings are extremely common in processed foods, candies, sodas, chips, and flavored snacks because they are cheaper and more consistent than natural ones.
The Difference Between Natural and Artificial — A Key Nuance

Here is something important: a natural flavoring and an artificial flavoring can taste nearly identical, and sometimes even the same chemical compound is involved. The distinction is really about where it came from — nature or a lab — not necessarily about whether it is healthier, safer, or better-tasting. This is a common point of confusion.

The word "flavoring" can be used in two ways, and both are correct:

1. As an uncountable noun (no "a," no plural)
Here, it refers to the general concept of adding flavor — the act or idea of flavoring, or the presence of flavoring as a quality.

"This dish contains no artificial flavoring."
"The sauce gets its depth from flavoring added during cooking."

2. As a countable noun ("a flavoring" / "flavorings")
Here, it refers to a specific, individual substance used to flavor something.

"Vanilla is a common flavoring in baking."
"The product contains several flavorings to mimic the taste of real fruit."
"They used two different flavorings: one for sweetness, one for tartness."

Both uses are standard. The countable form is more common when you are talking about specific, identifiable substances. The uncountable form is more common when speaking in a general or abstract way.

Understanding the word family helps you use it correctly:

  • Flavor (noun) — the actual taste/smell experience itself. "This soup has a rich flavor." Flavor is what you experience.
  • To flavor (verb) — the action of adding something to change the taste. "She flavored the rice with saffron."
  • Flavored (adjective) — describes something that has had flavor added to it. "Strawberry-flavored milk."
  • Flavoring (noun) — the substance or ingredient that does the flavoring. "Vanilla extract is the flavoring she used."

Think of it this way: you flavor food using a flavoring, and the result is flavored food with a particular flavor.
Where You Will See the Word

Flavorings appear constantly in everyday life:

  • On food packaging labels: ingredients lists often read "natural flavoring," "artificial flavoring," or just "flavoring."
  • In recipes: a recipe might say "add a few drops of almond flavoring."
  • In food journalism and health writing: discussions about whether artificial flavorings are safe, what "natural flavoring" really means on a label, etc.
  • In industrial food production: manufacturers use flavorings extensively to make processed foods taste consistent.

Less commonly, "flavoring" can be used figuratively (non-literally) to mean anything that adds a distinctive quality, tone, or character to something — not just food.

"The film had a jazz flavoring throughout its soundtrack."
"His speech had a slight political flavoring that made some people uncomfortable."

Here, "flavoring" means a subtle quality that colors the overall experience, the same way a vanilla flavoring colors the taste of a cake. This use is metaphorical, but it follows naturally from the core meaning.

A flavoring is a substance — either natural or artificial — that is added to food or drink to create, enhance, or change its taste and smell; and by extension, it can also refer figuratively to anything that adds a distinctive character or quality to something.
